newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German private drugs groups ripe for consolidation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German private drugs groups ripe for consolidation.

text.p: As a wave of consolidation in the global chemicals and pharmaceutical industry gains momentum it may soon engulf privately-owned German companies, riding high on their reputations as very attractive targets.

Family-owned German drugs and chemicals groups, boasting high-profile products, promising research, a large sales force and billions of marks in annual sales, have long enjoyed their relative obscurity, insisting it will always stay that way.

But news in late May that privately-held Boehringer Mannheim, a major player in the international diagnostics market, was snapped up by Swiss industry giant Roche AG for $11 billion sent tremors through the industry.

Not only will the deal, which catapults the German-Swiss duo to global co-leader in diagnostics with U.S. group Abbott Labs, speed up the race for new targets among the industry giants, it will widen the scope for smaller groups, industry insiders believe.
PRIVATE FIRMS MORE ACCESSIBLE AND ACQUISITIVE

The news indicated a turning point had been reached -- either privately-held firms were becoming more accessible than ever before or they were actively scouting out the chances for making acquisitions themselves.

"Yes (the Boehringer Mannheim-Roche deal) was a shock," Hans Joachim Langmann, chairman of Merck KGaA, another family-owned drugs group, told Reuters in an interview, suggesting other families might now feel tempted by high-ticket takeover offers.

International powerhouses like Roche, scouring the world for new targets with an appetite for some of the elusive private German groups, might now be in a better position to strike a deal at the top prices they would be willing to pay.
"People have lots of money and they are searching for targets especially in the very key German market," said Virginia Pascoe, a pharmaceutical sector analyst at James Capel in London.

Although Boehringer Mannheim was nearly as well known for its boardroom battles as for its leading position in the global diagnostics market, news that the Engelhorn family had sold now after surviving very rocky years came out of the blue.

It did, however, illustrate a relatively minor but still significant point -- families are having greater difficulties keeping their various members content while at the same time finding successful managers who suit them.

As the 71-year-old Boehringer Mannheim scion Curt Engelhorn appeared tired of slugging it out with warring relatives, analysts say there may be more elderly owners more willing to sell if only to end the headaches about how to run the firm.
"Some companies may have spotted the fact they cannot carry the burden alone anymore," said Andreas Schmidt, analyst at BZW in Frankfurt.
PRODUCTS AND SALES OUTLETS THE KEY
The more important issue however is a firm's viability, measured partly through management but more conventionally through products and how and where the group sells these.
"There comes a point where in order to reach critical mass, these companies will have to do something," said Thomas Schiessle, analyst at Delbrueck & Co. in Frankfurt.
A case in point might be the Bad Homburg-based Altana ATLG.F group, which last week saw its share price jump over eight percent in one day, in part on rumours off an impending sale.

However since Altana, majority-owned by the founder's daughter Susanne Klatten, steadfastly denies all talk of any impending sale, analysts said the company would have to adopt another tactic -- go on the offensive and buy something itself.
For Altana, posting sales of 2.28 billion marks ($1.3 billion) last year, analysts said it was critical to find another pillar for growth besides its gastro-intestinal drug Pantoprazol.

Facing the "buy or be bought" dilemma exposes another problem for smaller private German companies as they often lack the financial firepower to buy something big enough to push them into the industry's top tier.
Besides the often prohibitively high purchase costs, analysts said a second problem is often how small German companies might integrate their bigger conquests.

Consequently privately-owned firms are often back to square one -- agreeing to a sale at a time when industry giants are on the prowl and the small fish can still dictate some terms, or accepting the role of a small player.
SCHWARZ PHARMA WANTS TO BUILD RESEARCH

Schwarz Pharma AG, which floated a portion of its shares two years ago and quickly advanced to a market darling, is one such company facing a problem after altering its strategy. It no longer wants to earn money largely through its successful sales force but also plans to build up innovative research capacities too.
Yet analysts identify Schwarz Pharma as a particularly astute company which truly believes in boosting shareholder value and taking appropriate action.
"I think Patrick Schwarz-Schuette (chief executive) is savvy enough to either merge, sell or tap the capital markets at right moment," said an analyst who asked not to be named.
GOING PUBLIC ANOTHER OPTION
Going public would be another option for these small companies, but appears not to have caught on as only Merck and Schwarz Pharma have floated some shares recently.
Analysts have often said the dynamic German pharmaceuticals markets was not accurately reflected with its very small number of groups producing drugs only.
As pressures on the international giants including German powerhouses Hoechst AG and Bayer AG increase, analysts say it is no longer possible to speculate about which company might link up with whom.
"These days it its possible for anyone to match with almost anyone else," said Markus Rausch, analyst at Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt.

But even as the restructuring picks up speed and analysts predict an even bigger shakeout looms, Merck's Langmann said families might still try to hold on to their stake, if only to avoid the tremendous tax payments they would face.
Speaking about the family that owns Altana, Langmann said: "I think they would incur prohibitively high tax payments which might make such a deal quite undesirable."
NICHE AREAS AND REGIONAL PLAYERS

And some well-run business might well try to hold out and establish themselves in niche areas and as regional players, especially as Germany's economy is expected to pick up and initial first scares about health-care reforms pass.
Even as analysts consider Merck, for example, as too large to be called small and needing to beef up its power, chief executive Langmann says he had absolutely no intention of shifting strategies.

Content with establishing itself in certain niche markets as a very strong player, Langmann proudly said "we are playing in the second league and quite frankly we do not care what happens in the first league."
"For us, this process of consolidation is not going to prove to be negative."
